However, as mentioned previously, these regularization techniques are less commonly used in practice for deep neural networks. Yet another popular regularization technique is early stopping: essentially treating the number of training steps (one forward-backward iteration) as a hyperparameter to be optimized on the validation set. Once the cost drops to a plateau in the validation set as a function of training steps, we will stop training even if further training will decrease the cost on the train set further. Last but not least, there is the powerful technique of dropout (Srivastava et al., 2014): randomly removing non-output nodes of a network for each minibatch's iteration (typ­ ically input nodes are included with probability of 0.8, hidden nodes are included with probability of0.5). One simple way to pass information from the previous features and labels from timestep t - 1 to tis to feed the output of h(t - 1) as input to h(t). We may envision a network at t that looks like Figure 3.10. Since the time series is assumed stationary (if not, ML won't work), we can force all U, V, and W (the weights connecting the hidden nodes) to be the same at every t. During training, all the features and labels up to t - 1 would be available and are used to indirectly determine h( t - 1) as they will affect the values of U, V, and W. Every time we advance a time step to t, the network adds another input node, hidden node, and output node. Since weights are presumed the same throughout the network, there is no problem in making a prediction at t. Once we have the actual label y(t), we can retrain the network and adjust all the weights (if we want to). We have just motivated one prototypical recurrent neural network (RNN). Most books display the RNN by rotating our figure 90° counterclockwise so that time proceeds on the horizontal axis (as is common in stock price charts) and the output is at the top, as in Figure 3.11. Notice the resemblance with a Hidden Markov Model. During prediction , you can think of the previous inputs x from 1 to t - 1 as modifying a hidden state h(t - 1) that serves as another input to h(t) and affecting the prediction y(t),just like the hidden state in a HMM that determines the probability distribution of the emissions x(t). A few key differences between standard HMMs and RNNs are that RNNs can model more complex mappings for state evolution and predictions (from states to observation ) using neural networks .
